evidence_set: Between fall 1971 and spring 1972, cannabis (marihuana or hashish) use was reported by 27% of the New York State high-school panel group who were exclusive legal-drug users and were currently using cigarettes, hard liquor and beer/wine at the fall survey (past 30 days; Table 2 labels total N≥342), compared with 2% of those who had never used any drug at that survey (total N≥467). These are survey-weighted percentages; no statistical tests, uncertainty intervals or covariate-adjusted estimates accompany these Table 2 percentages. Note 4 describes weights for school/homeroom selection probabilities and school response, plus high-school-panel reweighting after linkage loss to reproduce the time-1 marijuana-use frequency in the complete cross-sectional sample.

The paper uses crucial-step language for cannabis in the abstract (p. 912) and crucial-step/crucial-stage language in the running text (p. 913), not only in the abstract. The body also says that a particular drug does not invariably lead to drugs higher in the sequence, that many youths stop or regress, and that the stages are probably culturally determined (p. 914). Note 3 adds that the specific number of stages varies with the classification of drug behaviors used in an analysis. Thus the strong crucial-step/stage language and the caveat about non-invariable progression both occur within the body of the paper (editorial reading), alongside the separate classification caveat in the notes.
